          Abstract
          Matsuo, H, Funasaki, K, and Yamada, S. The applicability of the risk score approach to competitive sport: development of a physical
          success score for the Canadian football league combine. J Strength Cond Res 36(3): 695–701, 2022—In the scouting combine of
          the Canadian Football League (CFL), players are measured for 6 athletic abilities, including 2 measurements of body size. For
          coaches and their players who desire to play in the CFL, knowing the players metrics that are important for being drafted and their
          levels will help coaches plan and evaluate their training. Thus, the purpose of this study was to provide a simple scoring system using
          the predictors of CFL Combines identified by multivariate analysis and their regression coefficients, and reference values. In this
          study, authors created a scoring system to classify draft success and failure of CFL Combines based on the measurement results.
          This scoring system was named as the physical success score (PSS). To do so, a repeated grid-search cross-validation for variable
          selection algorithm was performed on the players (line: n 5 211, big skill linebacker, running back and tight end: n 5 177, skill
          [defensive back and wide receiver]: n 5 231) who participated in the CFL Combines between 2011 and 2019. The final binary
          logistic regression models and the reference values were used to generate the PSS for each group. As a result, PSS of the line, big
          skill, and skill were developed. In each group, all possible total scores and the estimated draft success probability were shown. From
          the results of this study, it was concluded that the PSS approach can provide useful information for coaches in setting training goals.
          Key Words: goal setting of training, multivariate analysis, scoring system

 "evidenceSummary":"Secondary analysis of publicly posted Canadian Football League (CFL) Combine results and draft outcomes (2011 to 2019) for three position groups: line (n = 221), big skill (n = 177) and skill (n = 231). Binary logistic models with repeated cross-validation produced a physical success score for each group, with mean validation AUCs of 0.77 (line), 0.76 (big skill) and 0.83 (skill), compared with 0.71, 0.67 and 0.78 for a classification tree benchmark.",
 "screeningLimitations":"The outcome is drafted or not, not performance in the field, and the scores come from one league's past combine selections without external validation. The paper's own AUC figures are inconsistent between sections, so the discrimination estimates are approximate.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could read a high score or a predicted draft probability as a forecast for an individual player's draft or career, when the model describes past combine selections and omits skill.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2022,
   "citation":"Matsuo H, Funasaki K, Yamada S. The applicability of the risk score approach to competitive sport: development of a physical success score for the Canadian Football League combine. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2022;36(3):695-701.",
   "doi":"10.1519/jsc.0000000000004047",
   "abstract":"The authors built a simple scoring system, the physical success score (PSS), from CFL Combine measures to classify draft success for three position groups. Cross-validated logistic models identified the predictors and reference values for each group.",
   "tldr":"Position-specific score tables link combine measures such as height, mass and 40-yard sprint time to draft selection, and show the draft probability for each total score. Use them as reference points for goal setting, not as a prediction for any one player.",
   "methods":"Combine data (40-yard dash, bench press, vertical jump, broad jump, shuttle run, 3-cone drill, height and mass) and binary draft outcome were taken from public CFL records for players in three position groups. Repeated grid-search cross-validation selected predictors for a logistic model, and each measure was scored by category against a base category, with draft probability estimated for every possible total score.",
   "findings":"The final models included height, mass and 40-yard sprint in all groups, with bench press in the big skill and skill groups and 3-cone in the line and big skill groups; the 40-yard sprint was significant in all three models. Validation AUCs for the PSS were 0.77 (line), 0.76 (big skill) and 0.83 (skill), above the classification tree benchmark (0.71, 0.67 and 0.78). The score tables show, for example, a line total score of 2.0 corresponding to a draft probability of 79.5 to 90.5 percent.",
   "limitations":"The outcome is drafted or not, regardless of round, so it does not measure playing success. The abstract gives 211 line players, while the Methods and Table 4 give 221. The validation AUCs in the Methods (0.81, 0.79 and 0.88) differ from those in the Results (0.77, 0.76 and 0.83), and the model was not tested on independent players. Only complete data were used, and the competition level is not stated beyond draft candidates. The authors describe the scores as reference values for size and athletic ability, not skill.",
   "practicalImplications":"Coaches can use the position-specific tables to see which combine-style measures (height, mass, 40-yard sprint, and for some groups bench press or 3-cone) relate to draft selection, and what a total score implies. Use the tables as goal reference points and progress markers, since they describe past selections and exclude skill.",
   "athleteDev":"For performance staff working with gridiron prospects, the tables give position-specific targets for body size, 40-yard speed and strength or agility. The largest gaps between an athlete's results and the target bands show where to focus training, while skill assessment has to be done separately because the scores do not measure it.",
   "rtp":"This study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It relates combine-day test results to draft selection in prospects and does not address injury, rehabilitation or return to play."
 }
}

 "evidenceSummary":"Narrative review (no search method is described) of the limb symmetry index (LSI) and asymmetry index used after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction. The authors propose four considerations: choose the benchmark carefully, because the postinjury contralateral limb can itself be affected; treat movement asymmetries as task-dependent and variable; measure task performance and movement strategy alongside the LSI; and assess both limbs against a sport-specific envelope of function.",
 "screeningLimitations":"The review has no described search, so the choice of supporting studies cannot be checked, and the authors state that the evidence for the LSI in return-to-sport decisions is mixed. The envelope-of-function approach is presented as a proposal, and the authors say the evidence base for return-to-sport testing is in its infancy.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could treat the four considerations as a validated replacement for LSI cut-offs, when the paper gives no new pass or fail thresholds and calls for future research to test them.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2024,
   "citation":"Jordan MJ, Bishop C. Testing limb symmetry and asymmetry after anterior cruciate ligament injury: 4 considerations to increase its utility. Strength and Conditioning Journal. 2024;46(4):406-414.",
   "doi":"10.1519/ssc.0000000000000821",
   "abstract":"The limb symmetry index is widely used to judge recovery after anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury, but the evidence supporting it for return-to-sport decisions is mixed. The authors outline four considerations for improving its use, including benchmark choice, task-dependent movement asymmetry, movement strategy, and an envelope-of-function approach.",
   "tldr":"Do not rely on a single limb symmetry percentage after ACL injury. Pair it with a benchmark that suits the athlete, measure both limbs across several tests and movement strategies, and judge readiness against the sport's demands.",
   "methods":"Narrative review of the scientific literature on limb symmetry and asymmetry indices after ACL reconstruction, with practical considerations drawn from that literature. No systematic search or quantitative synthesis is described.",
   "findings":"The authors argue that the postinjury contralateral limb is a poor default benchmark because ACL injury can reduce its strength and function, which can inflate the LSI. 24	symptoms, and (5) functional status.
25	Methods A cross-sectional survey study was conducted using the ResearchMatch platform. The key independent variable
26	was age of first exposure to football (AFE < 12 versus AFE ≥ 12). Main outcomes included depressive symptoms (Patient
27	Health Questionnaire-9; PHQ-9), anxiety symptoms (Generalized Anxiety Disorders-7; GAD-7), cognitive difficulties (Brit-
28	ish Columbia Cognitive Complaints Inventory; BC-CCI), Neurobehavioral Symptom Inventory (NSI) score, and prevalence
29	of other health problems. Multivariable regressions were assessed for associations between AFE and outcome variables.

31	4.2 ± 2.7 years of exposure to football, with an average AFE of 11.7 ± 3.1 years. In multivariable analyses, AFE < 12 was

36	problems or independent functional status.

The Association Between Age of First Exposure to American
Football at a Young Age and Later‑Life Health Issues in Healthy,
Community‑Dwelling Adults
Grant H. Rigney1,2 · John E. Dugan2,3 · Anthony Bishay2,4,5 · Soren Jonzzon2,5 · Jacob Jo2,4,5,6 · Kristen L. Williams2,5 ·
Scott L. Zuckerman2,5 · Douglas P. Terry2,5

Accepted: 20 April 2025
© The Author(s) 2025


Abstract
Introduction Younger age of first exposure (AFE) to American Football (football) is associated with later-life health problems
among former professional athletes in several studies; however, studies examining amateur (i.e., nonprofessional) athletes
are less clear.
Objective In a cohort of former amateur American Football players, this study assessed whether AFE to football was associ-
ated with: (1) psychiatric and neurobehavioral symptoms, (2) cognitive difficulties, (3) general health problems, (4) motor
symptoms, and (5) functional status.
Methods A cross-sectional survey study was conducted using the ResearchMatch platform. The key independent variable
was age of first exposure to football (AFE < 12 versus AFE ≥ 12). Main outcomes included depressive symptoms (Patient
Health Questionnaire-9; PHQ-9), anxiety symptoms (Generalized Anxiety Disorders-7; GAD-7), cognitive difficulties (Brit-
ish Columbia Cognitive Complaints Inventory; BC-CCI), Neurobehavioral Symptom Inventory (NSI) score, and prevalence
of other health problems. Multivariable regressions were assessed for associations between AFE and outcome variables.
Results In total, 107 male participants with exposure to football (mean age: 60.6 ± 15.1 years) reported an average of
4.2 ± 2.7 years of exposure to football, with an average AFE of 11.7 ± 3.1 years. In multivariable analyses, AFE < 12 was
not a significant predictor of PHQ-9 (unstandardized beta, B: 0.51, standard error, SE: 1.25, p = 0.682), GAD-7 (B: 0.09,
SE: 0.95, p = 0.926), NSI (B: − 0.56, SE: 2.93, p = 0.850), or BC-CCI (B: − 0.65, SE: 0.77, p = 0.403). However, more prior
concussions were associated with worse PHQ-9 (B: 0.44, SE: 0.10, p < 0.001), GAD-7 (B: 0.33, SE: 0.07, p < 0.001), NSI
(B: 1.04, SE: 0.23, p < 0.001), and BC-CCI scores (B: 0.26, SE: 0.06, p < 0.001). AFE < 12 did not predict general health
problems or independent functional status.
Conclusions AFE to football was not associated with adverse psychiatric, cognitive, neurobehavioral, or general health
outcomes among young, former amateur American Football players. However, more lifetime concussions were associated
with adverse cognitive and psychiatric health outcomes. Future studies should examine similar outcomes in older cohorts
with more comorbidities to further minimize potential confounding between general health and lack of later-life symptoms.

{
 "id":"Q55",
 "sourceFile":"The Association Between Age of First Exposure to American Football at a Young Age and Later-Life Health Issues in Healthy, Community-Dwelling Adults.pdf",
 "decision":"INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason":"",
 "degradedReason":"",
 "doiMissing":false,
 "identityCheck":"The title 'The Association Between Age of First Exposure to American Football at a Young Age and Later-Life Health Issues in Healthy, Community-Dwelling Adults' and authors (Rigney, Dugan, et al.) in the text match the filename and the Crossref title; the DOI is also printed on the first page.",
 "confidence":"high",
 "studyDesign":"Cross-sectional Study",
 "primaryDomain":"Brain Health & Psychology",
 "domains":["Brain Health & Psychology","Sports Medicine & Injury","Athlete Wellbeing"],
 "audiences":["Sports Medicine","Athletic Training","Performance","Research & Analytics","Coaching"],
 "sports":["American Football"],
 "populations":["Male Athletes","Healthy Athletes","Adult / Recreational"],
 "evidenceSummary":"Cross-sectional online survey of 107 men (mean age 60.6 years) with amateur American football exposure, recruited through the ResearchMatch registry. After adjusting for age, number of concussions and total years of football, starting before age 12 was not a significant predictor of depression, anxiety, neurobehavioral, cognitive, general health, motor or functional outcomes (for example PHQ-9 B = 0.51, p = 0.682), while more lifetime concussions were associated with worse PHQ-9, GAD-7, NSI and BC-CCI scores.",
 "screeningLimitations":"The design is cross-sectional, with retrospective self-reported exposure and symptoms from registry volunteers, so recall bias and selection are likely. The under-12 group was younger (mean 53 versus 65 years), and the authors note that age and general health could mask later-life effects, so the null result for age of first exposure is not strong evidence of safety.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could read the null age-of-first-exposure result as proof that early tackle football is harmless, when the study has 41 players in the under-12 group, a mean age of 60, and no measure of when or how the concussions occurred.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2025,
   "citation":"Rigney GH, Dugan JE, Bishay A, Jonzzon S, Jo J, Williams KL, et al. The association between age of first exposure to American football at a young age and later-life health issues in healthy, community-dwelling adults. Sports Medicine. 2025.",
   "doi":"10.1007/s40279-025-02239-w",
   "abstract":"In 107 former amateur American football players, starting to play before age 12 was not associated with depressive, anxiety, neurobehavioral, cognitive, general health, motor or functional outcomes after adjustment. A greater number of lifetime concussions was associated with worse psychiatric, cognitive and neurobehavioral scores.",
   "tldr":"Among healthy former amateur players, starting football before age 12 was not linked to worse later-life mood, cognition or health scores, but more lifetime concussions were. Use this as evidence that concussion burden matters, not as a green light for early tackling.",
   "methods":"Cross-sectional online survey of men with at least one year of amateur American football participation who were recruited through the ResearchMatch registry. Multivariable linear and logistic regressions adjusted for age, number of lifetime concussions and total years of football for depression (PHQ-9), anxiety (GAD-7), neurobehavioral symptoms (NSI), cognitive complaints (BC-CCI), and general health, motor and functional outcomes.",
   "findings":"Of 107 analysed men (41 with age of first exposure under 12, 66 with 12 or older), age of first exposure under 12 did not predict PHQ-9 (B = 0.51, p = 0.682), GAD-7 (B = 0.09, p = 0.926), NSI (B = -0.56, p = 0.850) or BC-CCI (B = -0.65, p = 0.403). Each additional lifetime concussion was associated with higher PHQ-9 (B = 0.44), GAD-7 (B = 0.33), NSI (B = 1.04) and BC-CCI (B = 0.26) scores, all p < 0.001. More concussions were also associated with higher odds of sleep problems (OR 1.30) and chronic pain (OR 1.91). Unadjusted differences in PHQ-9, GAD-7 and sleep problems favoured the older-starting group but were not significant after adjustment.",
   "limitations":"The cross-sectional, self-report design cannot show cause, and recall of exposure and concussions may be inaccurate. Participants were registry volunteers, mostly white and college-educated, and only those with complete surveys and no neurological disease were analysed. The under-12 group was small and younger, and the age-12 cut-off was chosen by the authors. Other contact sport exposure was not adjusted for, and the authors note the results may differ in older, less healthy or professional players.",
   "practicalImplications":"This study does not show that starting football before age 12 is safe or unsafe. The finding that more lifetime concussions went with worse mood, cognitive, sleep and pain scores supports keeping an accurate concussion history for each player and managing head impacts carefully at every age. Explain to parents that the study cannot answer their question about long-term risk of early starts.",
   "athleteDev":"For performance and medical staff, the study supports recording each athlete's full concussion history and reviewing it when planning contact load. It does not address on-field performance, and it does not identify a safe starting age for football.",
   "rtp":"This study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It surveyed generally healthy former players about lifetime concussions and later symptoms, not recovery from a current injury. Its link between concussion count and later symptoms should not be used to set return-to-play timelines."
 }
}

 "sourceFile":"The Association Between Age of First Exposure to American Football at a Young Age and Later-Life Health Issues in Healthy, Community-Dwelling Adults.pdf",
 "decision":"INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason":"",

 "doiMissing":false,
 "identityCheck":"The title 'The Association Between Age of First Exposure to American Football at a Young Age and Later-Life Health Issues in Healthy, Community-Dwelling Adults' and authors (Rigney, Dugan, et al.) in the text match the filename and the Crossref title; the DOI is also printed on the first page.",
 "confidence":"high",
 "studyDesign":"Cross-sectional Study",
 "primaryDomain":"Brain Health & Psychology",
 "domains":["Brain Health & Psychology","Sports Medicine & Injury","Athlete Wellbeing"],
 "audiences":["Sports Medicine","Athletic Training","Performance","Research & Analytics","Coaching"],
 "sports":["American Football"],
 "populations":["Male Athletes","Healthy Athletes","Adult / Recreational"],
 "evidenceSummary":"Cross-sectional online survey of 107 men (mean age 60.6 years) with amateur American football exposure, recruited through the ResearchMatch registry. After adjusting for age, number of concussions and total years of football, starting before age 12 was not a significant predictor of depression, anxiety, neurobehavioral, cognitive, general health, motor or functional outcomes (for example PHQ-9 B = 0.51, p = 0.682), while more lifetime concussions were associated with worse PHQ-9, GAD-7, NSI and BC-CCI scores.",
 "screeningLimitations":"The design is cross-sectional, with retrospective self-reported exposure and symptoms from registry volunteers, so recall bias and selection are likely. The under-12 group was younger (mean 53 versus 65 years), and the authors note that age and general health could mask later-life effects, so the null result for age of first exposure is not strong evidence of safety.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could read the null age-of-first-exposure result as proof that early tackle football is harmless, when the study has 41 players in the under-12 group, a mean age of 60, and no measure of when or how the concussions occurred.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2025,
   "citation":"Rigney GH, Dugan JE, Bishay A, Jonzzon S, Jo J, Williams KL, et al. The association between age of first exposure to American football at a young age and later-life health issues in healthy, community-dwelling adults. Sports Medicine. 2025.",
   "doi":"10.1007/s40279-025-02239-w",
   "abstract":"In 107 former amateur American football players, starting to play before age 12 was not associated with depressive, anxiety, neurobehavioral, cognitive, general health, motor or functional outcomes after adjustment. A greater number of lifetime concussions was associated with worse psychiatric, cognitive and neurobehavioral scores.",
   "tldr":"Among healthy former amateur players, starting football before age 12 was not linked to worse later-life mood, cognition or health scores, but more lifetime concussions were. Use this as evidence that concussion burden matters, not as a green light for early tackling.",
   "methods":"Cross-sectional online survey of men with at least one year of amateur American football participation who were recruited through the ResearchMatch registry. Multivariable linear and logistic regressions adjusted for age, number of lifetime concussions and total years of football for depression (PHQ-9), anxiety (GAD-7), neurobehavioral symptoms (NSI), cognitive complaints (BC-CCI), and general health, motor and functional outcomes.",
   "findings":"Of 107 analysed men (41 with age of first exposure under 12, 66 with 12 or older), age of first exposure under 12 did not predict PHQ-9 (B = 0.51, p = 0.682), GAD-7 (B = 0.09, p = 0.926), NSI (B = -0.56, p = 0.850) or BC-CCI (B = -0.65, p = 0.403). Each additional lifetime concussion was associated with higher PHQ-9 (B = 0.44), GAD-7 (B = 0.33), NSI (B = 1.04) and BC-CCI (B = 0.26) scores, all p < 0.001. More concussions were also associated with higher odds of sleep problems (OR 1.30) and chronic pain (OR 1.91). Unadjusted differences in PHQ-9, GAD-7 and sleep problems favoured the older-starting group but were not significant after adjustment.",
   "limitations":"The cross-sectional, self-report design cannot show cause, and recall of exposure and concussions may be inaccurate. Participants were registry volunteers, mostly white and college-educated, and only those with complete surveys and no neurological disease were analysed. The under-12 group was small and younger, and the age-12 cut-off was chosen by the authors. Other contact sport exposure was not adjusted for, and the authors note the results may differ in older, less healthy or professional players.",
   "practicalImplications":"This study does not show that starting football before age 12 is safe or unsafe. The finding that more lifetime concussions went with worse mood, cognitive, sleep and pain scores supports keeping an accurate concussion history for each player and managing head impacts carefully at every age. Explain to parents that the study cannot answer their question about long-term risk of early starts.",
   "athleteDev":"For performance and medical staff, the study supports recording each athlete's full concussion history and reviewing it when planning contact load. It does not address on-field performance, and it does not identify a safe starting age for football.",
   "rtp":"This study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It surveyed generally healthy former players about lifetime concussions and later symptoms, not recovery from a current injury. Its link between concussion count and later symptoms should not be used to set return-to-play timelines."
 }
}

                                                                                                              Abstract
                                                                                                              Clarke, R, Read, PJ, De Ste Croix, MBA, and Hughes, JD. The deceleration deficit: a novel field-based method to quantify
                                                                                                              deceleration during change of direction performance. J Strength Cond Res 36(9): 2434–2439, 2022—The study investigated the
                                                                                                              relationship between linear and change of direction (COD) speed performance components and the individual differences between
                                                                                                              deceleration deficit (DD) and COD deficit (CODD). Thirty-six subjects (mean 6 SD: age 5 20.3 6 2.9 years; stature 5 175.2 6 7.7

                                                                                                              cm; and body mass 5 78.0 6 16.7 kg) completed 3 trials of a 505 test in both turning directions (dominant [D]; nondominant [ND])
                                                                                                              and 3 15-m linear sprints. Deceleration deficit was calculated by the 15-m approach in the 505 test, minus the athlete’s linear 15-m
                                                                                                              sprint time. To compare individuals CODD and DD, z-scores were calculated, and moderate worthwhile changes (MWCs) were
                                                                                                              identified between these deficit z-scores. Significant correlations were identified between linear sprints and 505 time (D: r 5 0.71,
                                                                                                              0.74; P , 0.01. ND: r 5 0.76, 0.75; P , 0.01) for 10-m and 15-m sprint. respectively, and between 505 performance and CODD (D:
                                                                                                              r 5 0.74; P , 0.01. ND: r 5 0.77; P , 0.01) and DD (D: r 5 0.41, P , 0.05. ND: r 5 0.44, P , 0.01). Deceleration deficit was
                                                                                                              significantly related to CODD (D: r 5 0.59; P , 0.01. ND: r 5 0.62; P , 0.01); however, 78% of subjects demonstrated differences
                                                                                                              between these deficit measures greater than an MWC. In conclusion, linear speed has the strongest significant relationship with 505
                                                                                                              performance. Deceleration deficit could provide a more isolated construct than CODD which may be related to an athlete’s
                                                                                                              deceleration capabilities.

   "doi":"10.1519/jsc.0000000000003856",
   "abstract":"The study compared a new field-based deceleration deficit (DD) with the established change-of-direction deficit (CODD) and linear sprint speed in 36 athletes. Linear speed was strongly related to 505 time but not to either deficit, while DD was only moderately related to CODD and 505 time.",
   "tldr":"Linear speed explained 505 time better than either deficit measure in this sample. DD may show braking ability that CODD hides, since the two disagree for most athletes, so check both, per turning direction, before deciding what limits an athlete.",
   "methods":"In one session, 36 university-level invasion-sport athletes completed three 505 trials in each turning direction and three 15-m sprints with timing gates. DD was the 505 approach time minus the 15-m sprint time, and CODD was the 505 time minus the 10-m sprint time. Pearson correlations and z-scores with a moderate worthwhile change threshold compared the measures.",
   "findings":"Linear sprint times correlated with 505 time (r = 0.71 to 0.76), while neither 10-m nor 15-m sprint time was related to CODD or DD. CODD correlated with 505 time (r = 0.74 to 0.77), and DD correlated with 505 time (r = 0.41 to 0.44) and with CODD (r = 0.59 to 0.62). A moderate worthwhile change between the two deficit z-scores was seen in 78 percent of athletes in at least one turning direction.",
   "limitations":"The study is a single-session cross-sectional correlation with 36 athletes, and the authors state that the reliability and validity of DD still need testing. No force-plate data were collected, so the braking contribution cannot be measured directly. The paper describes the sample as both recreationally active and competitive university-level, and the authors caution that results may not carry over to other performance levels. Most DD correlations are below 0.5, so DD shares only about a fifth of its variance with the measures it was compared against.",
   "practicalImplications":"Use the 505 test with a 15-m sprint in the same session to separate linear speed from braking ability, and compare DD with CODD for each turning direction. When the two deficits disagree, the athlete may need work on deceleration rather than on acceleration or the turn. Because the metric is not yet tested for reliability, use the flag to guide further assessment, not as a fixed training prescription.",
   "athleteDev":"For performance staff, the study supports testing linear speed and deceleration separately instead of relying on total 505 time or CODD alone. Look at both turning directions, since the paper shows the two deficits often disagree. Track how athletes respond to any deceleration-focused work, because the paper does not show that training DD changes change-of-direction performance.",
   "rtp":"This study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It tested currently uninjured athletes in one session and did not assess injured athletes, rehabilitation or change in deceleration after injury. Do not use DD as a return-to-sport or change-of-direction clearance criterion."
 }
}

103	 ABSTRACT
104	
105	
106	
107	Training with low-load exercise performed under blood-flow restriction can augment muscle
108	
109	hypertrophy and maximal strength to a similar extent as the classical high-load strength training
110	
111	method. However, the blood-flow restriction method elicits only minor neural adaptations. In an
112	
113	attempt to maximize training-related gains, we propose using other protocols that combine high
114	
115	voluntary activation, mechanical tension and metabolic stress.
116	                                                                 D
117	                       EP
118	SUMMARY for Table of Contents: In an attempt to maximize training-related gains in
119	
120	
121	
122	
123	                         TE
124	maximal strength and muscle hypertrophy, we propose to design new protocols that combine
125	
126	high mechanical tension and metabolic stress.
127	
128	
129	
130	
131	KEY WORDS: Mechanical tension; metabolic stress; blood flow restriction; muscle
132	
133	            C
134	hypertrophy; neural adaptations
135	
136	
137	
138	 C
139	A
140	 KEY POINTS
141	
142	   Mechanical tension and metabolic stress contribute to training-related muscle hypertrophy
143	
144	    and increases in maximal strength.
145	
146	   As the magnitude of the neural adaptations after low-load exercise with blood flow
147	
148	    restriction are less than those elicited by high-load strength training and this method is
149	
150	    difficult for some individuals and insufficient for well-trained athletes, we suggest there is a
151	
152	
153	
154	
155	    need for new strength-training protocols.
156	                                                                   D
157	    One training option is to combine different levels of mechanical tension and metabolic stress
158	
159	
160	
161	
162	                        EP
163	    that are optimized to the training status of the individual.
164	
165	
166	
167	
168	                          TE
169	            C
170	    C
171	A
172	 INTRODUCTION
173	
174	The increase in muscle strength is classically based on the "overload" principle (1). This
175	
176	principle, which states that a minimal load/contraction intensity must be exceeded during the
177	
178	training sessions to increase muscle strength, is used in sport training and in clinical and
179	
180	rehabilitation settings. Based on this concept, moderate-to-high mechanical loading of the
181	
182	muscle (≥60-70% of the one repetition maximum - 1RM) has long been considered as the main
183	
184	
185	                                                                D
186	stimulus (i.e., mechanical tension) for muscle hypertrophy and thereby an increase in muscle
187	
188	strength (2-4). More recently, however, studies using training loads of less than 50% of 1RM
189	
190	
191	
192	
193	                        EP
194	performed until failure (5) or with blood-flow restriction (BFR) (ischemic/hypoxic condition)
195	
196	have reported gains in maximal strength and comparable levels of muscle hypertrophy to that
197	
198	
199	
200	
201	                          TE
202	observed with conventional heavy-load strength training (for recent reviews, see 6-8). These
203	
204	studies suggested that the accumulation of fatigue-related metabolites (i.e., metabolic stress) may
205	
206	play a role in the exercise stimulus leading to an increased accretion of muscle mass and strength
207	
208	(9-10).
209	
210	
211	
212	             C
213	The current Perspective for Progress paper compares training programs performed with high
214	
215	
216	
217	  C
218	loads to those involving low loads under BFR and the adaptations elicited by each approach. As
219	
220	one of the objectives was to examine the possible contribution of metabolic stress on muscle
221	
222	
223	
224	A
225	hypertrophy, we chosen to compare low-load exercise with BFR to high-load strength training,
226	
227	as the former method produce more metabolic stress and needs fewer repetitions to reach failure
228	
229	(i.e. greater efficacy) than low-load training performed under normal blood circulation (5). We
230	
231	also explore the utility of the approach of combining moderate-to-high loads (mechanical stress)
232	
233	and brief rest intervals between sets (metabolic stress) to maximize muscle hypertrophy and
234	 strength gains in untrained and trained individuals. Although the efficacy of low-load training
235	
236	with BFR is particularly relevant for patients and healthy untrained or aged individuals, for
237	
238	whom heavy-load strength training may be problematic and contra-indicated (6-8,11,12), such
239	
240	training may be insufficient in well-trained athletes who require high level of strength or power
241	
242	(13).
243	
244	
245	
246	
247	                                                               D
248	Although increases in maximal strength are due to both muscle and neural adaptations, the
249	
250	purpose of our article is not to provide an in-depth review of the molecular mechanisms
251	
252	
253	
254	
255	                       EP
256	underlying muscle hypertrophy, nor to discuss the numerous neural adaptations induced by
257	
258	strength training. Such information can be found in the following reviews on muscle (13-17) and
259	
260	
261	
262	
263	                         TE
264	neural (18-22) adaptations.
265	
266	
267	
268	HIGH-LOAD STRENGTH TRAINING VS. LOW-LOAD EXERCISE WITH BFR
269	
270	Muscle adaptations to high-load strength training
271	
272	Based on a substantial literature on traditional strength training, the American College of Sport
273	
274	            C
275	Medicine (2) recommends the use of moderate loads (70-85% of 1RM, 8-12 repetition per set for
276	
277	
278	
279	  C
280	1-3 sets per exercise) for novice and intermediate individuals and high loads (70-100% of 1RM,
281	
282	1-12 repetitions per set for a minimum of 3-6 sets per exercise) for trained athletes to increase
283	
284	
285	
286	A
287	both muscle hypertrophy and maximal strength.
288	
289	
290	
291	High mechanical loading of the muscle (≥70% of 1RM) is traditionally considered to be an
292	
293	essential stimulus for increases in maximal strength (2-5,21,23). At the muscle level, the primary
294	
295	adaptation is an increase in muscle size (i.e., hypertrophy). Strength training increases force
296	 capacity by increasing the quantity of contractile proteins in individual muscle fibers and thereby
297	
298	the cross-sectional area of muscle. In pennate muscles (e.g., gastrocnenmii, vastus medialis and
299	
300	lateralis), however, the angle of pennation of muscle fascicles increases with strength training
301	
302	(24,25), which reduces the force contributed by each fiber to the tendon (longitudinal force
303	
304	vector) due to an increase in the oblique angle of pull. The training-related increase in the force
305	
306	produced by individual muscle fibers in pennate muscles, therefore, is attenuated by increases in
307	
308	
309	                                                                D
310	the pennation angle (22,24). The magnitude of this adaptation likely explains some of the
311	
312	variability between muscle strength and anatomical cross-sectional area seen among individuals.
313	
314	
315	
316	
317	                        EP
318	Although it has been instructed for a long time that muscle hypertrophy is greater when the
319	
320	
321	
322	
323	                          TE
324	exercise involves a moderate load (~70% of 1RM) with many repetitions than a higher load
325	
326	(>80% 1RM) with fewer repetitions (2,26,27), more recent publications do not support that
327	
328	claim, at least in untrained or medium-trained individuals (see 5). The meta-analysis by
329	
330	Schoenfeld and colleagues (5) even indicates that similar gains in muscle hypertrophy can be
331	
332	obtained for a large range of loads (~30–80% of maximum) provided that sets are performed to
333	
334	             C
335	failure. A load equal to 20% of 1RM appears, however, insufficient to promote muscle
336	
337	
338	
339	 C
340	hypertrophy (28). In contrast, greater gains in maximal strength are observed for training with
341	
342	higher load (> 60% of 1RM) compared with lower load (≤ 60% of 1RM). The relative greater
343	
344	
345	
346	A
347	increase in maximal strength than in muscle hypertrophy with high-load training is usually
348	
349	explained primarily by a greater contribution of neural changes (2,18,21) and muscle cytoskeletal
350	
351	remodelling associated with force transmission (29).
352	 Muscle adaptations to low-load exercise under BFR
353	
354	In the mid-1990s, it was suggested that the accumulation of fatigue-related metabolites may
355	
356	contribute to an increased accretion of muscle mass and maximal strength (9,10). This idea was
357	
358	supported by subsequent studies showing that training with loads ranging from 20 to 50% of
359	
360	1RM performed under BFR increased muscle hypertrophy and maximal strength (30,31). In
361	
362	these studies, blood flow was restricted to a muscle group by the application of external pressure
363	
364	
365	                                                               D
366	via a tourniquet, an inflated cuff, or an elastic band applied over the proximal portion of either
367	
368	the upper or lower extremities. This external pressure varied across muscle groups and studies,
369	
370	
371	
372	
373	                       EP
374	but typically ranged from 60 to 270 mmHg (7). In most conditions, the external pressure applied
375	
376	around the limb was sufficient to maintain some arterial flow, but blocked venous blood return
377	
378	
379	
380	
381	                         TE
382	distal to the occlusion site (32). Such reduction in blood flow induces an ischemic/hypoxic

                          TE
             C
  C
A
 ABSTRACT



Training with low-load exercise performed under blood-flow restriction can augment muscle

hypertrophy and maximal strength to a similar extent as the classical high-load strength training

method. However, the blood-flow restriction method elicits only minor neural adaptations. In an

attempt to maximize training-related gains, we propose using other protocols that combine high

voluntary activation, mechanical tension and metabolic stress.
                                                                 D
                       EP
SUMMARY for Table of Contents: In an attempt to maximize training-related gains in




                         TE
maximal strength and muscle hypertrophy, we propose to design new protocols that combine

high mechanical tension and metabolic stress.




KEY WORDS: Mechanical tension; metabolic stress; blood flow restriction; muscle

            C
hypertrophy; neural adaptations



 C
A
 KEY POINTS

   Mechanical tension and metabolic stress contribute to training-related muscle hypertrophy

    and increases in maximal strength.

   As the magnitude of the neural adaptations after low-load exercise with blood flow

    restriction are less than those elicited by high-load strength training and this method is

    difficult for some individuals and insufficient for well-trained athletes, we suggest there is a




    need for new strength-training protocols.
                                                                   D
    One training option is to combine different levels of mechanical tension and metabolic stress




                        EP
    that are optimized to the training status of the individual.




                          TE
            C
    C
A
 INTRODUCTION

The increase in muscle strength is classically based on the "overload" principle (1). This

principle, which states that a minimal load/contraction intensity must be exceeded during the

training sessions to increase muscle strength, is used in sport training and in clinical and

rehabilitation settings. Based on this concept, moderate-to-high mechanical loading of the

muscle (≥60-70% of the one repetition maximum - 1RM) has long been considered as the main


                                                                D
stimulus (i.e., mechanical tension) for muscle hypertrophy and thereby an increase in muscle

strength (2-4). More recently, however, studies using training loads of less than 50% of 1RM




                        EP
performed until failure (5) or with blood-flow restriction (BFR) (ischemic/hypoxic condition)

have reported gains in maximal strength and comparable levels of muscle hypertrophy to that




                          TE
observed with conventional heavy-load strength training (for recent reviews, see 6-8). These

studies suggested that the accumulation of fatigue-related metabolites (i.e., metabolic stress) may

play a role in the exercise stimulus leading to an increased accretion of muscle mass and strength

(9-10).



             C
The current Perspective for Progress paper compares training programs performed with high



  C
loads to those involving low loads under BFR and the adaptations elicited by each approach. As

one of the objectives was to examine the possible contribution of metabolic stress on muscle



A
hypertrophy, we chosen to compare low-load exercise with BFR to high-load strength training,

as the former method produce more metabolic stress and needs fewer repetitions to reach failure

(i.e. greater efficacy) than low-load training performed under normal blood circulation (5). We

also explore the utility of the approach of combining moderate-to-high loads (mechanical stress)

and brief rest intervals between sets (metabolic stress) to maximize muscle hypertrophy and
 strength gains in untrained and trained individuals. Although the efficacy of low-load training

with BFR is particularly relevant for patients and healthy untrained or aged individuals, for

whom heavy-load strength training may be problematic and contra-indicated (6-8,11,12), such

training may be insufficient in well-trained athletes who require high level of strength or power

(13).




                                                               D
Although increases in maximal strength are due to both muscle and neural adaptations, the

purpose of our article is not to provide an in-depth review of the molecular mechanisms




                       EP
underlying muscle hypertrophy, nor to discuss the numerous neural adaptations induced by

strength training. Such information can be found in the following reviews on muscle (13-17) and




                         TE
neural (18-22) adaptations.



HIGH-LOAD STRENGTH TRAINING VS. LOW-LOAD EXERCISE WITH BFR

Muscle adaptations to high-load strength training

Based on a substantial literature on traditional strength training, the American College of Sport

            C
Medicine (2) recommends the use of moderate loads (70-85% of 1RM, 8-12 repetition per set for



  C
1-3 sets per exercise) for novice and intermediate individuals and high loads (70-100% of 1RM,

1-12 repetitions per set for a minimum of 3-6 sets per exercise) for trained athletes to increase



A
both muscle hypertrophy and maximal strength.



High mechanical loading of the muscle (≥70% of 1RM) is traditionally considered to be an

essential stimulus for increases in maximal strength (2-5,21,23). At the muscle level, the primary

adaptation is an increase in muscle size (i.e., hypertrophy). Strength training increases force
 capacity by increasing the quantity of contractile proteins in individual muscle fibers and thereby

the cross-sectional area of muscle. In pennate muscles (e.g., gastrocnenmii, vastus medialis and

lateralis), however, the angle of pennation of muscle fascicles increases with strength training

(24,25), which reduces the force contributed by each fiber to the tendon (longitudinal force

vector) due to an increase in the oblique angle of pull. The training-related increase in the force

produced by individual muscle fibers in pennate muscles, therefore, is attenuated by increases in


                                                                D
the pennation angle (22,24). The magnitude of this adaptation likely explains some of the

variability between muscle strength and anatomical cross-sectional area seen among individuals.




                        EP
Although it has been instructed for a long time that muscle hypertrophy is greater when the




                          TE
exercise involves a moderate load (~70% of 1RM) with many repetitions than a higher load

(>80% 1RM) with fewer repetitions (2,26,27), more recent publications do not support that

claim, at least in untrained or medium-trained individuals (see 5). The meta-analysis by

Schoenfeld and colleagues (5) even indicates that similar gains in muscle hypertrophy can be

obtained for a large range of loads (~30–80% of maximum) provided that sets are performed to

             C
failure. A load equal to 20% of 1RM appears, however, insufficient to promote muscle



 C
hypertrophy (28). In contrast, greater gains in maximal strength are observed for training with

higher load (> 60% of 1RM) compared with lower load (≤ 60% of 1RM). The relative greater



A
increase in maximal strength than in muscle hypertrophy with high-load training is usually

explained primarily by a greater contribution of neural changes (2,18,21) and muscle cytoskeletal

remodelling associated with force transmission (29).
 Muscle adaptations to low-load exercise under BFR

In the mid-1990s, it was suggested that the accumulation of fatigue-related metabolites may

contribute to an increased accretion of muscle mass and maximal strength (9,10). This idea was

supported by subsequent studies showing that training with loads ranging from 20 to 50% of

1RM performed under BFR increased muscle hypertrophy and maximal strength (30,31). In

these studies, blood flow was restricted to a muscle group by the application of external pressure


                                                               D
via a tourniquet, an inflated cuff, or an elastic band applied over the proximal portion of either

the upper or lower extremities. This external pressure varied across muscle groups and studies,




                       EP
but typically ranged from 60 to 270 mmHg (7). In most conditions, the external pressure applied

around the limb was sufficient to maintain some arterial flow, but blocked venous blood return




                         TE
distal to the occlusion site (32). Such reduction in blood flow induces an ischemic/hypoxic

environment that may augment the training effect of the exercised muscle compared with the

normal blood-flow condition (30,31).



The gains in muscle size and strength achieved with low-load exercise training performed under

            C
BFR have been reported to be similar to those elicited by conventional heavy-load strength



 C
training. For example, Takarada and colleagues (31) reported that a 16-week (2 sessions/week)

low-load (50% of 1RM) exercise training of the elbow flexor muscles performed under BFR



A
(100 mmHg) increased muscle cross-sectional area (CSA) and strength (~19% and 18%,

respectively), which was similar to the increases (~15% and 22.5%) achieved with high-intensity

strength training (80% of 1RM) without BFR and much more than an identical low-intensity

(50% of 1RM) protocol without ischemia (~5% and 1%). Similar observations have been

reported with lower loads combined with BFR (20-30% of 1RM; 33-35). Even in athletes, low-
 load (20% of 1RM) training with the knee extensors performed under hypoxic or vascular-

occlusion conditions led to similar increases in maximal strength (14.8 vs. 13.3 %) and muscle

hypertrophy (6.1 vs. 6.6%) (36). This exercise stimulus, however, may be insufficient to increase

the 1RM load in well-trained athletes (37) as, for example, powerlifters (38).



Meta-analyses comparison


                                                                D
Depending of the inclusion criteria adopted, recent meta-analyses have reached slightly different

conclusions (6-8). One analysis on patients suffering from musculoskeletal disease (7) and




                        EP
another analysis on various population of individuals (8) both indicated that the increase in

muscle strength was less after low-load exercise training with BFR than with high-load strength




                          TE
training. In the latter meta-analysis (8), between-group comparisons indicated significantly

greater gains (~7%) in muscle strength for high-load strength training than for low-load exercise

training with BFR. Similar findings were observed when the gain in muscle strength was

Mechanical factors

Early animal studies found that mechanical tension acts as a primary mechanism for muscle

growth and thereby increases in muscle strength (for a review, see 39). For example, removal of

a synergist muscle (i.e., chronic overload) led to the hypertrophy of the remaining muscles (40)

and increases in the mechanical strain on a muscle attenuated the atrophy caused by unloading


                                                                 D
(41). Subsequent, studies found that imposing high mechanical tension and/or lengthening of

activated muscles is a major mediator of myofibril protein synthesis (42).




                        EP
Mechanotransduction and growth factors




                          TE
Muscle hypertrophy observed after chronic mechanical overload results from an increase in the

net protein synthesis and in the number of myonuclei that mediate the increase in the volume of

contractile proteins within a muscle fiber (15). The process by which the mechanical stress is

translated into chemical signals that trigger an intracellular signaling cascade leading ultimately

to the production of muscle proteins is known as mechanotransduction. Briefly, in presence of

             C
chronic muscle overload, focal adhesion kinases (FAK) bind to mechanoreceptors (i.e., integrin



  C
receptors) that connect the extracellular matrix to the sarcolemma. Through its action, FAK

converts mechanical tension into a chemical signal that mediates intracellular anabolic



A
(mammalian target of rapamycin complex 1 - mTORC1) and catabolic (family of transcription

factors - FOXO) pathways (for more details, see 15,16,43). When associated with sufficient

nutritional intake (15, 44), this process favors protein synthesis over its degradation, resulting in

a net increase in contractile protein and muscle-fiber hypertrophy (Figure 1; 16).
 [Figure 1]



The mTORC1 is not solely activated by high mechanical loads, but also other stimuli such as

insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1) and one of its variants termed mechanogrowth factor

(MGF). MGF is produced locally and contributes to up-regulate protein synthesis via the

activation of the P13K/Akt /mTORC1 pathway (for reviews see 15,16,43,45). Due of its rapid


                                                               D
expression following mechanical loading, MGF contributes to enhance the post-exercise

hypertrophic response and to facilitate local repair of muscle damage (Figure 1; 46), but its




                       EP
intervention does not seem to be obligatory for muscle growth (15,47).

              C

A

multiple sets training, which impacts the total training volume (2,118,121). In addition, more

            C
than 3 min of rest may be needed to maintain maximal strength and power during successive sets



 C
and to accumulate a high training volume, depending of the training status of the individual, the

muscle group being targeted, and the type of exercise (single vs. multi-joint exercise) performed



A
(17,118). A 3-min interval allows enough time for the resynthesis of phosphocreatine (PCr)

through the aerobic system (59) and the elimination of part of intracellular metabolic by-products

into the blood stream. When associated with limited O2 availability (i.e., hypoxia), these

alterations slow down the rate of PCr resynthesis and ADP rephosphorylation, which reduce both

the maximal strength and speed of contraction (59).
 Several studies have shown that rest intervals of 2-3 min result in significantly greater increases

in maximal strength and power compared with shorter rest intervals (30-90 s) (17,120,122-124).

Although necessary to maximize the level of voluntary activation and thereby maximal strength,

the maintenance of training intensity during successive sets is not usually chosen when

attempting to induce muscle hypertrophy (27). The experimental evidence on the influence of


                                                                 D
short (≤ 1 min) and long (≥ 3 min) inter-set intervals during strength training is mixed. Some

studies showed an advantage of long inter-set intervals for muscle hypertrophy (74,125), whereas




                        EP
others found either better result with short inter-set intervals (126) or no significant difference

(127,128).




                          TE
Unfortunately, the workout volume in the two training programs was not matched in all these

studies (74,128) which likely influenced the conclusion. In contrast, Goto and colleagues (60)

compared the outcomes achieved with a 12-week strength training program for two groups of

subjects who performed protocols that were matched for volume and load intensity (3-5 sets of

             C
10 reps at 70-75% of 1RM with an inter-set rest period of 1 min). One group performed the



  C
repetitions in each set without any interruption, whereas the other group had a 30-s rest period

after the first 5 repetitions of each set. As expected, blood lactate concentration was significantly



A
greater for the protocol that did not include the 30-s rest. The main finding was that muscle CSA

only increased significantly in the group that did not include a rest period during each set

indicating that a strength training protocol leading to high accumulation of metabolic by-product

may favour muscle hypertrophy.
 In search of new training strategies

Recent work from our laboratory has examined the effectiveness of a new training design (called

the 3/7 method) to promote strength gains in the bench press exercise performed by physically

active individuals (129). This method, based on a strength training protocol introduced by a

French coach named Emmanuel Légeard, is characterized by 5 sets of an incremental number of

repetitions per set (from 3 repetitions in the first set to 7 repetitions in the last set) with a constant


                                                                     D
load of ~70% of 1RM. Each set was separated by a very brief rest interval of 15 s. When

compared with the more "classical" method of a constant number of repetitions in each set and




                         EP
matching the load and number of repetitions (i.e., training volume; 4x6 method: 4 sets of 6

repetitions with 150-s rest interval between sets), the 3/7 method produced a significantly




                           TE
(p<0.05) greater increase in 1 RM load (29.8 vs. 21.8% for the 4x6 method) and maximal

strength (22.4 vs. 9.9% for the 4x6 method) as tested with an isokinetic device (Ariel

Computerized Exercise System, Ariel Dynamic Inc.) after 12 weeks (2 sessions/week) of training

(129). Doubling the number of sets performed with the classical method (i.e., 8 sets of 6

repetitions) slightly increased (p<0.05) the gain in 1RM load (35.9%) compared with the 3/7

              C
method, but the increase in maximal strength did not differ (p>0.05) between the two protocols



  C
(25.5 vs. 22.4%). Also, the increase in peak power was greater (p<0.05) for the 8x6 (21.6%)

compared with the 3/7 (16.3%) method, but the difference was not significant (p>0.05) when



A
volume was matched for the two protocols (i.e., 3/7 vs. 4x6) (129).



Subsequently, we examined the relative contributions of neural and muscular adaptations to the

gains achieved by the elbow flexors after a 12-week (2 sessions/week) training program with a

load of 70% of 1RM performed by moderately trained individuals (130). Training involved a total
 of ~50 repetitions in each session in an attempt to optimize the dose/response (see 17). The 3/7

protocol was repeated twice with a 150-s rest between the two bouts and compared with the 8x6

method; 150 s of rest between sets. Our results indicated that both protocols (3/7 and 8x6)

increased the 1RM load (22.2 vs. 12.1%; p<0.05) and MVC force during an isometric contraction

(15.7 vs. 9.5%; p<0.05) with a greater increase in 1RM load (p<0.05) and marginally greater

MVC force (p=0.07) for the 3/7 method.


                                                                D
The EMG activity of two elbow flexors (long head of biceps brachii and brachioradialis),




                        EP
normalized to their respective maximal M wave (Mmax) elicited by supramaximal electrical

stimulation of the motor nerve, increased (p<0.05) with no difference between training methods




                          TE
(14.5 vs. 8.1%; p>0.05). Despite the limitations of this normalization procedure (131,132), it

reduces the confounding influence of differences in recording conditions (electrodes placement)

and peripheral changes (subcutaneous tissues, muscle mass and architecture) between

experimental sessions. In contrast, biceps brachii thickness, as measured by ultrasonography,

increased to a greater extent (9.6 vs. 5.5 %; p<0.05) for the 3/7 method. To verify that the brief

             C
inter-set interval and the incremental number of repetitions in the successive sets in the 3/7 method



  C
compromised O2 delivery to the active muscles, we compared the changes in tissue oxygenation

with near-infrared spectroscopy in biceps brachii and brachioradialis for the 3/7 and 8x6 method



A
(133). Our data indicated a greater average deficit in oxygenation for the 3/7 method and, in

contrast to the 8 x 6 method, an absence of recovery on O2 content between sets.



More recently, we compared the 3/7 method to a protocol that reversed the order of the sets (i.e.,

7/3 method), similar to a drop-set protocol. Our findings indicated that the gains in 1RM load,
 MVC force, and muscle thickness were significantly less (p<0.05) for the 7/3 method compared

with the 3/7 method (Figure 2). Although the normalized EMG amplitude of the elbow flexors

increased (p<0.05) after both methods, the training gains did not differ significantly.



[Figure 2]




                                                                  D
Together, these observations demonstrate that brief inter-set intervals and incremental increases

in the number of repetitions performed in successive sets, results in superior outcomes for the 3/7




                        EP
method compared with the 8x6 and 7/3 methods.




                          TE
The greater stimulus for muscle hypertrophy associated with the 3/7 method raises questions

about the underlying mechanisms. As observed for low-load exercise training under BFR,

shortening the inter-set intervals during high-volume strength training with moderate loads

increases the metabolic stress and the acute hormonal response (82,134). Although a short inter-

set rest interval (1 min) blunts the rate of myofibrillar protein synthesis in the early post-exercise

             C
recovery period, but not ~24 h later, compared with longer rest period (5 min) (81), there is no



  C
clear evidence of an association between an acute increase in myofibrillar protein synthesis after

a training session and muscle hypertrophy after a strength training program (135,136). The



A
suggestion of Schoenfeld and colleagues (17) that inter-sets of ≤ 1 min are likely too brief to

promote maximal hypertrophic gains may depend on differences in training variables, such as the

total workout relative to the training status of the individual (60,70) and, in particular for trained

athletes, the number of sets performed to failure (137,138). With the 3/7 method, the failure

stage is reached during the last two sets. The greater gains in 1RM load, MVC force, and muscle
 thickness for the 3/7 protocol compared with the 7/3 protocol (same training volume and inter-set

rest interval) are consistent with this hypothesis as the 7/3 protocol does not produce task failure.



These findings indicate that the effectiveness of the 3/7 method results from a protocol that

combines moderate-to-high mechanical tension and metabolic stress (Figure 3). In addition to

producing muscle hypertrophy, the 3/7 method also appears to elicit neural adaptions that


                                                                  D
contribute to increases maximal strength. Additional experiments are needed to optimize the

training variables (workout volume; optimal rest interval for mono vs. pluri-articular and upper




                        EP
vs. lower body exercises, free weight vs. machine; …) and to determine the relative roles of

mechanical tension and metabolic stress in contributing to the outcomes. On a practical point of




                          TE
view, a major advantage of the 3/7 method is its greater efficacy (amount of progress relative to

the total number of repetitions) over more classical methods.



[Figure 3]



             C
PERSPECTIVES FOR PROGRESS



  C
Over the last two decades, our concepts and practice of strength training methods have been

strongly shaken. One example is that training with low-load exercise performed until failure or



A
under BFR may augment muscle protein synthesis (139,140), muscle hypertrophy and maximal

strength (25,26,28) to a similar extent as achieved with high-load low volume training in both

untrained individuals and trained athletes (for meta-analyses, see 5-8). Another recent change in

dogma is that bodybuilding-type training (moderate load, high volume, and brief inter-set

interval) is likely not the best strategy to augment muscle protein synthesis and thereby the
 increases in muscle growth (see 138). Among many others, these two examples have led to

numerous questions at both mechanistic and practical levels.



Mechanisms of action

A major advance in this field is the observation of an acute increase in muscle protein synthesis

within a few hours (4-6 h that remains elevated for more than 24 h) after exercise provided


                                                               D
nutrition is adequate (see 15,16,135). Unfortunately, the association between the amount of

increase in muscle protein synthesis observed in acute condition and its translation into muscle




                        EP
hypertrophy after long-term training remains to be defined (135,136). It is also not clear how

successive sessions within a training program, and thus their frequency (number of




                          TE
sessions/week), modulates in fine the amount of muscle growth.



One of several possible explanations for the lack of association between muscle hypertrophy and

protein synthesis is the way in which muscle CSA is measured. Classically, measures of

anatomical CSA or muscle thickness are used to assess the amount of muscle hypertrophy. In

            C
pennate muscles, however, a more functional measure is the physiological CSA (141), which can



 C
be accomplished with ultrasonography when the angle of pennation is taken into consideration.

Moreover, muscle CSA can be influenced by changes in other factors, such as muscle fiber



A
swelling in response to training-related damage or modifications in the characteristics of

connective tissues (135). Future studies need to assess more carefully the translation of elevated

levels of protein synthesis into muscle hypertrophy.
 Another issue that needs more attention is the role of anabolic hormones in training-induced

adaptations (see 14,50,80,135,136). Many studies have reported a transient increase in the levels

of hormones in the blood (testosterone, GH, IGF-1) and their relative concentrations seems to

depend of several exercise variables, such as the type of exercise (mono- vs. multi-articular), the

workout volume, the inter-set interval (72,118), and whether or not the exercise is performed

under BFR (13). Although mechanistic studies suggest that these hormones do not play a direct


                                                                 D
role in muscle protein synthesis (15,16,73), they may have an indirect influence by promoting

satellite cell activation and fusion (45,50,80). As exercise-related increases in the levels of these




                        EP
hormones is relatively modest compared with their exogenous administration, it would be useful

to determine their dose-dependent effects in both women and men and the influence of various




                          TE
training protocols. The field needs clear experimental designs to establish the functional role, if

any, of increases in blood hormone concentrations in acute and long-term adaptations.



Although low-load exercise training with BFR is a valid and safe method to increase muscle

hypertrophy and strength in frail and sarcopenic patients (see 6,7,12,55), the functional

             C
consequences for healthy sedentary and older individuals and especially for athletes needs to be



  C
established. As already mentioned, neural adaptations (i.e., voluntary activation and muscle

coordination) play an important role in improving maximal and functional strength (e.g., chair-



A
rise), but these adaptations are not evident after low-load exercise training with or without BFR.

As an example, sedentary and older individuals are typically not able to achieve the maximal

level of voluntary activation (142), which reduces their ability to develop maximal strength

capacity unless they perform strong contractions on a regular basis (143). Training studies need

to distinguish between muscle and neural adaptations to identify the relative training-related
 responses to low-load and high-load exercises. Approaches are to use electrophysiological

methods, such as the superimposed twitch technique, to quantify activation-related adaptations

(144) or more insightful methods (see 18) to obtain information on adaptive mechanisms.



In addition to maximal strength, the development of explosive strength (rate of force

development/power) is necessary for many athletes and for older persons so that they produce a


                                                                 D
reactive response as quickly as possible when balance is compromised (145). Training with rapid

contractions increases both the level of voluntary activation (146) and muscle-tendon stiffness




                        EP
(147). Increases in muscle-tendon stiffness, which improve the rate at which force is transmitted

to the skeleton (148), can be improved by employing high-load concentric or eccentric




                          TE
contractions (149,150) and stretch-shortening-type contractions (151,152). As exercise training

under BFR involves low loads and is performed slowly, there are currently no clear evidences

that this training modality is effective to increase muscle-tendon stiffness substantially (35,153).



Practical aspects

             C
In absence of a clear association between muscle hypertrophy and the levels of metabolic stress



  C
as the consequence of the ischemic/hypoxic environment (11,154), Pearson and Hussain (13)

suggested that the influence of mechanical tension and metabolic stress may be additive (Figure



A
3). However, the relative contributions of these primary factors are not known. Also, the gains

achieved by combining high-load and low-load exercises with BFR in the same session or in

separate sessions need to be compared with a program of moderate-load strength training with

brief inter-set intervals (such as the 3/7 method). Well-designed studies are needed to investigate

whether it is more effective to optimize the effects of mechanical tension and metabolic stress by
 combining low-load exercise with BFR and high-load strength training or to use a protocol with

moderate loads and brief inter-set intervals to induce a high level of metabolic stress. An

alternative approach, as used by competitive athletes for many years, is to periodize (block

training) complementary methods throughout a long-term training program (2). Here also,

investigations are needed to determine the most appropriate protocol or the best combination of

protocols.


                                                                D
An additional practical criterion that needs to be considered for persons who have time




                        EP
constraints, is the benefit to cost ratio (amount of progress relative to the time spent during

training) of the different protocols. This is also critical for well-trained athlete to improve the




                          TE
efficacy of their training programs and to limit the risk of overtraining. In this context, the 3/7

protocol is appealing as one bout of a given exercise can be completed in ~1.5 min.



In conclusion, recent studies reporting contradictory findings to our well-established knowledge

have challenged contemporary concepts about strength training. This uncertainty should be used

             C
as an opportunity to advance the field by augmenting our knowledge on the adaptive



 C
neuromuscular mechanisms of strength and power training, and by offering more consistent

guidelines. As the neuromuscular adaptations are modulated by numerous criteria (e.g., age, sex,



A
individual training status and experience, workout volume, number of sessions per week, and

muscle group), much remains to be done to determine the optimal training dose that maximizes

the performance gains achieved by persons with varying characteristics.
 Acknowledgments

The authors thank Prof. Roger Enoka for editing a draft version of the manuscript. No funding

was received for this paper. The authors have no conflict of interest to disclose

   "abstract":"Low-load training under blood-flow restriction (BFR) can increase muscle size and maximal strength about as well as heavy-load training, but it produces only minor neural adaptations. The authors propose protocols that combine high voluntary activation, mechanical tension and metabolic stress.",
   "tldr":"Low-load BFR training builds size and strength but adds little neural adaptation and may not be enough for well-trained athletes. The paper argues for combining high mechanical tension with metabolic stress, for example through brief inter-set rests, but this needs testing in more groups.",
   "methods":"Perspective-style narrative review. The authors compare high-load training with low-load BFR training, discuss the mechanisms of hypertrophy and neural adaptation, summarise meta-analyses, and present their own 3/7 method studies against comparison protocols.",
   "findings":"Meta-analyses found BFR training effective for strength, but a high-load advantage of about 7% appeared in one analysis and not in another, depending on inclusion criteria. Low-load BFR training produces only minor neural adaptations, and the mechanisms of its hypertrophy effect remain unresolved.",
   "limitations":"The narrative format means the literature selection cannot be checked, and the paper leans on the authors' own studies, whose sample sizes are not given in the text. Figure 3 is a hypothetical model, and the meta-analyses disagree on BFR versus heavy-load strength gains. Crossref lists 2021, but the PDF prints 2020 on the copyright line and marks the article as published ahead of print, so 2020 is kept. No volume or page numbers are printed.",
   "practicalImplications":"Low-load BFR training looks usable for patients and for untrained or older adults, but the paper judges it probably insufficient for well-trained athletes who need high strength or power. For athletes, the authors suggest combining heavy loads and moderate loads with brief rests, or periodising complementary methods, with the choice guided by time available and the athlete's training status.",
   "athleteDev":"For strength coaches, the paper suggests that well-trained athletes should not rely on low-load BFR alone for maximal strength. It offers two options: heavier loads with longer rests for maximal strength, and moderate loads with brief rests (the 3/7 method, about 1.5 min per exercise bout) for muscle size and time efficiency. Test any new protocol on your own athletes first, since the 3/7 evidence comes from active and moderately trained people.",
   "rtp":"This review cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. Its rehabilitation content is limited to the statement that low-load BFR training is valid and safe for frail and sarcopenic patients, which does not set return-to-play criteria for athletes. Do not use the BFR evidence to set post-injury loading targets for athletes."

17	Abstract
18	Background Neuromuscular profiling (NP) provides an objective means of assessing neuromuscular function to guide
19	targeted training interventions. However, coaching terminology used to describe NP outputs (e.g., ‘explosive’, ‘springy’) is
20	often inconsistently defined or applied, leading to misinterpretation and limiting effective use. Variations in how NP metrics
21	are calculated and interpreted further complicate comparisons across studies and practical applications. Despite their wide-
22	spread use in sport science and performance settings, no framework currently exists to evaluate whether the terminology
23	and interpretations associated with NP metrics accurately represent measured outputs and intended neuromuscular traits.
24	Objectives This review aimed to evaluate whether terms/labels used across six commonly applied NP methods—Dynamic
25	Strength Index, Eccentric Utilisation Ratio, Force–Velocity Profile, Impulse Analysis, Reactive Strength Index, and Reactive
26	Strength Index Modified—accurately represent the neuromuscular characteristics they are intended to measure. A second-
27	ary objective was to identify methodological limitations that may affect the interpretation, standardisation, and practical
28	application of these methods.
29	Methods A systematic search of PubMed, Scopus and SPORTDiscus identified 1653 eligible studies, of which 184 met
30	inclusion criteria. A modified quality scale was used to assess study relevance. Extracted data included reported output val-
31	ues, assigned terms/labels, underlying mechanisms, and supporting evidence. Results were grouped by explanatory themes,
32	with terms/labels identified and examined based on the underlying mechanisms they were intended to represent. Findings
33	were then synthesised to identify patterns in terminology, interpretation, and limitations.
34	Results A total of 209 NP methods were evaluated (147 ratio-based, 62 non-ratio-based). NP interpretation was task-depend-
35	ent and influenced by methodological variability. Inconsistency was found in the terminology, definitions, and calculations
36	used to derive NP metrics. Several studies attempted to classify athletes based on NP metrics, though few accounted for
37	constituent components in interpretation. Commonly used terms/labels included: ‘explosive/explosiveness’ (indicating greater
38	rate of force development), ‘spring/springy’ (suggesting effective stretch–shortening cycle utilisation), ‘stiff/compliant’
39	(representing a continuum of lower extremity stiffness), and ‘strong/weak’ (reflecting maximal force production capability).
40	Conclusions This review offers a consolidated synthesis of NP terminology, interpretation, and methodological considera-
41	tions. Clarifying terminology and addressing limitations may improve communication between researchers and practitioners,
42	supporting more standardised use of NP tools.
